content.p: In the early hours of 10 June 1942, German police and SS units surrounded the Czech mining village of Lidice, a place with a church, a school, a few farms and a little over 500 people. By that afternoon, according to Smithsonian Magazine, 173 men had been executed. The women were taken away, the children were separated from them three days later, and the buildings were burned and blown up. The Nazi authorities had promised to wipe the name of Lidice off the map of Europe. The village was razed as a reprisal for the attack on Reinhard Heydrich, the acting Reich Protector in Prague, although the US Holocaust Memorial Museum says there was no real evidence linking the villagers to the men who carried it out.

The Germans did not hide what they had done. They announced it on the radio and filmed it. The result was the opposite of what they intended: Lidice became one of the best-known symbols of Nazi brutality, and the film they shot was later shown to the judges at Nuremberg.
content.h2: An ordinary village in an occupied country
content.p: The Lidice Memorial traces the village back to a chronicle entry of 1318. Its church of St Martin dates from 1352, and the school appears in records from 1713. The growth of coal mining and iron-making around nearby Kladno turned the village into a working mining community in the second half of the nineteenth century: 270 inhabitants in 33 houses in 1848, 506 people in 50 houses by 1890. A travel writer visiting the site describes it in 1942 as an unremarkable Czech village, of no strategic importance, where life went on much as usual apart from the occasional German soldier.

The wider country was under a harsh regime. Heydrich, a senior SS figure, became deputy Reich Protector of Bohemia and Moravia in September 1941. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum says that he oversaw severe occupation policies, including the persecution of Czech Jews, and tried to stamp out Czech culture. The Lidice Memorial says about 5,000 people described as resisters or their helpers were imprisoned during his short rule, and that people were executed under martial law, some without trial, to spread fear.

According to the Holocaust Museum, Heydrich's killing was planned in London by the British Special Operations Executive together with the Czechoslovak government-in-exile under Edvard Beneš, under the code name Operation Anthropoid. Nine Czechoslovak resistance members parachuted into the country on the night of 28 December 1941; two of them, Jan Kubiš and Jozef Gabčík, were given the task of killing Heydrich.

On 27 May 1942 in a Prague street, Gabčík's submachine gun jammed as Heydrich's car slowed for a bend, and Kubiš threw a bomb that exploded near the rear wheel. Heydrich was not killed outright, but shrapnel led to septicaemia, and he died on 4 June. Hitler, says the museum, demanded the killing of up to 10,000 Czechs. Karl Hermann Frank, the senior SS and police leader in the Protectorate, flew to Berlin and argued against so drastic a step because it could interfere with long-term economic and political plans. Frank, the museum stresses, had no intention of going easy on the Czechs: he declared martial law on 27 May and began a manhunt.

Accounts of what pointed the Germans toward Lidice differ in detail but agree that the pretext was thin. The Lidice Memorial says a letter addressed to a woman working in a factory at Slaný was held back by the factory's co-owner, J. Pála, and that its vague contents made the Gestapo in Kladno suspect a link between the assassination and the Horák family of Lidice, with a son in the Czechoslovak forces in Britain. Smithsonian Magazine describes a love letter intercepted by the Gestapo and says the woman, on interrogation, implicated the Horáks. Both accounts agree that searches found nothing: no weapons, no transmitter, nothing compromising. Living Prague says that Stanislav Horak and his wife were arrested on 4 June.

The Holocaust Museum calls the choice of Lidice "somewhat arbitrary". Desperate for leads, the Germans picked the village named in the letter. On 9 June, the day of Heydrich's state funeral in Berlin, Hitler ordered it destroyed. The Lidice Memorial says the shooting of the men was carried out on the orders of K. H. Frank. The Holocaust Museum describes the German claim that two Lidice families were connected to the assassins as false.

German forces surrounded the village on the night of 9 to 10 June and ordered the roughly 500 residents to assemble, according to the Holocaust Museum. Men and boys of 15 and older were separated from the women and younger children. The sources do not agree on the cut-off age: the Lidice Memorial and the Holocaust Museum say 15 or older, History.com and Private Prague Guide say 16.

The women and children were taken to the village school, and then to a grammar school gymnasium in Kladno. The men were taken to the Horák farm. Smithsonian Magazine says they were brought out in groups of ten and shot against a barn covered with mattresses to stop ricochets. The same article says that the village priest, Josef Stembarka, was offered mercy if he would calm his congregation, and refused, saying: "I have lived with my flock," and "now I will die with it." Living Prague also says that the priest was among the men shot.

The total for the day is 173 men and boys, a figure given by the Holocaust Museum, the Lidice Memorial, Smithsonian Magazine, Living Prague and Private Prague Guide (History.com says more than 170). Smithsonian Magazine adds that women who refused to leave their husbands were shot, and that men who happened to be away were later found and killed. The museum says seven women were shot alongside the men of their families and that more than 20 other Lidice residents were shot at a shooting range in Prague in the following weeks. Prisoners from the Terezin camp are said to have dug the mass grave for the dead men.

After three days in Kladno the children were taken from their mothers. The Holocaust Museum says that of 203 women from Lidice, most of those 16 or older were deported to Ravensbrück concentration camp, and 53 of them died in the Nazi camp system before the end of the war. History.com puts the number who died at Ravensbrück at about 50, with three recorded as disappeared.

The children were sent to Łódź in occupied Poland. Pregnant women and babies under one year were separated early, Smithsonian Magazine says; the Lidice Memorial records that infants and children chosen for German families were taken away from the rest. At Łódź, personnel from the SS Race and Settlement Main Office measured and examined the children. Nine were judged to have the "Germanic" features the SS wanted, according to both the museum and Smithsonian Magazine, and were sent to a group home in occupied Poland. They were given German names, taught German and placed by the Lebensborn programme with adoptive German parents.

The remaining children were murdered. The Holocaust Museum says approximately 80 were gassed at the Chełmno killing center. Smithsonian Magazine says 81 children arrived there on 2 July and that historians believe they were killed in mobile gas vans that same day. Private Prague Guide, which counts 105 children in the village, says the youngest was a year and six days old, that the children were told to undress for a "shower" and that death took about eight minutes. Living Prague and Smithsonian Magazine give 82 as the number of children who never returned, the number memorialised today. The figures differ slightly from source to source.

Once the village was empty the Germans set its houses on fire and then levelled them, with explosives used on what remained, according to the Lidice Memorial. They destroyed the church. They also destroyed the cemetery: Living Prague says bodies were pulled from coffins, valuables taken, and gravestones broken up and used as foundations for army buildings. By 1943, according to the Memorial, all that was left was an empty space marked with notices forbidding entry.

German propagandists filmed the work. The Holocaust Museum says the film includes blazing houses, buildings being demolished and German officials posing among the ruins, and that it was meant to show the cost of resisting German rule. German radio reported the destruction with pride. Smithsonian Magazine quotes the broadcast of the following day: "All male inhabitants have been shot. The women have been transferred to a concentration camp. The children have been taken to educational centers. All houses of Lidice have been leveled to the ground, and the name of this community has been obliterated." The Memorial's current director, Martina Lehmannová, told the magazine that the Nazis publicised the destruction because "they were proud of it".

Lidice was not the only place that suffered. The Holocaust Museum says Ležáky, a village of about 50 people, was treated in a similar way. On 24 June 1942 its adult residents were shot, thirteen children were taken to Łódź, two sisters were chosen for Germanization, and the rest were killed, probably at Chełmno. Private Prague Guide links Ležáky to a resistance group called Silver A, which kept radio contact with London, and says its transmitter had been near the village.

The museum gives the larger toll of the reprisals as 3,188 Czechs arrested and 1,327 sentenced to death, with thousands of Jews from Prague deported to Lublin and other camps. On 18 June, SS and police found Kubiš, Gabčík and other resistance fighters in an Orthodox cathedral in Prague. Kubiš died of wounds from the fight; Gabčík and the others died by suicide, the museum says. Relatives of the assassins and of other resisters were sent to Mauthausen and killed. Historian Elizabeth White of the Holocaust Museum told Smithsonian Magazine that the reprisals achieved one of their goals: inside Czechoslovakia, "the massacre really did lead to the breaking of the resistance."

News of the destruction spread quickly. Stories appeared in international newspapers in mid-June, and the Holocaust Museum says Lidice became an international symbol of Nazi brutality. Smithsonian Magazine records the reaction of the US Navy secretary Frank Knox: "If future generations ask us what we were fighting for in this war, we shall tell them the story of Lidice." A neighbourhood in Joliet, Illinois, took the name Lidice, and President Roosevelt praised the gesture. In Stoke-on-Trent, the member of Parliament Barnett Stross led a "Lidice Shall Live" campaign that raised money for rebuilding. Several villages worldwide took the name, according to the Lidice Memorial, and many girls born at the time were named for it.

The magazine, quoting White, also argues that the Allies found Lidice a safe example to publicise: Lidice's victims could be presented as peaceful civilians and universal victims, while the Allies were wary of emphasising the persecution of Jews. That is the magazine's and the historian's reading, not a quotation from Allied policy documents.

At Nuremberg, the German film was shown to the International Military Tribunal as Document No. 379, according to the Lidice Memorial, and Allied prosecutors cited the destruction as an example of Nazi war crimes. Frank was arrested and stood trial in 1946 before the People's Court in Prague; the Holocaust Museum says he was convicted of many wartime crimes, including the destruction of Lidice and Ležáky, and that seven women from Lidice were among those who watched his execution. Two survivors, Marie Doležalová and Marie Hanfová, who had been nine and eleven in 1942 and had been put through Germanization, testified at the RuSHA trial in Nuremberg in 1947.

The survivors, according to the Lidice Memorial, were 143 women and 17 children; the memorial counts 340 Lidice citizens murdered. The children's return was slow. Václav Zelenka, aged eight, came back in 1947 as the last of the lost children and later became mayor of the rebuilt village, Smithsonian Magazine reports. The historian White describes returned children who had forgotten Czech and needed a translator to speak to their families. On 10 June 1945 the Czechoslovak government announced that Lidice would be rebuilt.

The foundation stone of the new village was laid in 1947 and the first houses begun in May 1948. The Lidice Memorial and Smithsonian Magazine put the distance from the old site at 300 metres; Private Prague Guide says about 150. The old site was preserved as a memorial with the common grave of the men. A rose garden, the Garden of Peace and Friendship, opened on 19 June 1955. Smithsonian Magazine says it holds more than 24,000 donated rose bushes, while the Memorial says thousands.

A museum opened at the site in 1962, and the International Children's Exhibition of Fine Arts has been held in Lidice since 1967. A sculpture of 82 faces, installed in 2000, honours the children who did not return; Living Prague says visitors still leave flowers and small toys at its base. In October 2012, after a letter in June marking the 70th anniversary, Germany's president, Joachim Gauck, visited Lidice, according to War History Online; in the letter he had expressed deep sorrow and said Germany accepted responsibility, and he met survivors during the visit. War History Online reported in February 2020 that when Miloslava Kalibová died, Jaroslava Skleničková was the only remaining survivor of the women of Lidice.
